AM22A-01.stem_issue: Significant figures: '5.0' and '4.0' liters suggest 2 s.f. yet the answer is asked to a tenth of a degree; harmless on ACT but slightly inconsistent. Otherwise clean.

bounds.bound: PV rises (pressure up 37.5%, volume down 20%: a test-wise student sees 165/120 outweighs 5/4) so T rises: answer > 23 C
Answer must be far from a 'Celsius-ratio' value: none readable without work

estimation_bound.interval: coarse 50-60 C (kills 25.3, 74.8; 60.0 sits on the coarse edge); finer pins 52.6

neighbouring_setup.what: applies the factor 1.1 to the Celsius temperature (23*1.1) - the exact trap the stem warns against; 74.8 = 296*1.175 - 273, i.e. adding the percent changes (+37.5% - 20% = +17.5%) instead of multiplying
neighbouring_setup.bound_kills: 25.3 survives the >23 bound (barely); neither is killed without work

AM22A-01.option_structure: No clear pattern; 60.0 I could not reconstruct from any natural error (60.0+273 = 333 = 296*9/8), so it reads as a filler value.
AM22A-01.free_elimination: None cheaper than solving; the ratio 660/600 = 1.1 is so clean that solving IS the one-step estimate.
AM22A-01.duplicate_note: Stock combined-gas-law with Celsius-to-Kelvin trap; very common in chemistry and SAT/ACT prep.
AM22A-01.domain_fit: Acceptable as Algebra (evaluate/rearrange a rational formula in context), but it is science-content-flavoured; ACT would more likely file it under Algebra/modeling. OK.

AM22A-02.stem_issue: Long but unambiguous. 'charged to the sellers' plus the explicit s = p-8 removes the incidence ambiguity.

bounds.bound: q = 400-5p: q is a multiple of 5 if p is a whole dollar - all four options are multiples of 5

estimation_bound.estimate: No-tax equilibrium 440 = 8p -> p = 55, q = 125; a tax lowers q. Price rises by 8*3/8 = 3 -> q drops 5*3 = 15 -> 110
estimation_bound.interval: q < 125 kills nothing (all options below); the one-step-finer incidence estimate gives 110 exactly

AM22A-02.arith_class: Partial: q = 3s-40 means q+40 is a multiple of 3 when the seller's amount s is a whole dollar. 95+40=135 and 110+40=150 pass; 100 and 105 fail. The stem does NOT state integer prices, so this narrows to two only for a student who assumes whole-dollar prices - flag as a soft integrality tell (95 vs 110).
AM22A-02.option_structure: Arithmetic progression 95, 100, 105, 110 (step 5) with the key at an END of the progression. None of the three distractors corresponds to an identifiable error I could find (tax added the wrong way gives 140, no tax gives 125, both absent), so the set reads as key minus 5/10/15 filler.
AM22A-02.free_elimination: Backsolving is about as cheap as solving: for each q compute p = (400-q)/5 and s = (q+40)/3 and test p-s = 8; 110 -> 58-50 = 8 on the first try if started from the end. Not materially cheaper. Integrality (above) cuts to 95/110 for free if integer prices are assumed.
AM22A-02.domain_fit: Yes - system of linear equations in context; genuine Algebra.

AM22A-03.stem_issue: 'at least 3 tablets for every laptop' is standard ACT phrasing; fine. Does not say the school must spend on tablets only to meet the ratio, but minimal tablets is the natural reading.

bounds.bound: Every laptop needs >= 3 tablets, so each laptop 'costs' at least 650+3*320 > 1500: L < 16 (a test-wise student does 24000/1500)

neighbouring_setup.what: Reverses the ratio (3 laptops per tablet: bundle 1950+320 = 2270, 24000/2270 = 10.6 -> 10 bundles); 12 = 24000/1950 (bundle of 3 laptops, ignoring tablets)
neighbouring_setup.bound_kills: neither killed by the no-work bound

AM22A-03.option_structure: 23 is far outside the cluster 10/12/14 and dies on sight; I could not reconstruct 23 from a natural error.
AM22A-03.free_elimination: Backsolve from the largest: 23 -> 23*1610 way over; 14 -> 22540 fits. Because the question asks for the GREATEST and 15 is not an option, finding the largest feasible option ends the item without checking 15 - roughly as cheap as solving, slightly cheaper for a weak student.
AM22A-03.domain_fit: Yes - linear inequalities in context; genuine Algebra.

bounds.bound: Compound >= simple interest: the multiplier exceeds the simple-interest multiplier 1.20 + 1.10 = 2.30, so P < 12000/2.3 = 5217.4. A test-wise student gets 2.30 with no exponent work.
Second deposit grows at least something: multiplier > 1.2155+1 -> P < 5416.3

estimation_bound.estimate: Coarse: simple interest 2.3 -> 5217 (lands ON a distractor); one step finer 1.2155+1.1025 = 2.318 -> 12000/2.318 = 5177

limiting_case.what: Second deposit earns nothing (12000/2.2155 = 5416.3) - the zero-growth extreme for deposit 2

neighbouring_setup.what: Exact answer under SIMPLE interest (12000/2.30); also sits exactly on the compound > simple bound

AM22A-05.option_structure: The key is the MINIMUM of the four options and every distractor corresponds to a weaker-growth model (simple interest, no growth on deposit 2, 5297 unreconstructed but also lower-growth). Because every error model under-counts growth, every distractor is larger than the key: 'pick the smallest' solves it. Serious structural tell.
AM22A-05.free_elimination: Yes, and far cheaper than solving: compute 1.20+1.10 = 2.30, note compound beats simple, so P < 12000/2.3 = 5217 - only 5177 survives. No powers of 1.05 needed. Item is broken as written; needs at least one distractor ABOVE the simple-interest line removed... i.e. distractors on both sides of the key (e.g. an over-counting error such as compounding deposit 2 for 4 years, 12000/2.431 = 4936).
AM22A-05.domain_fit: Borderline: exponential models in context are usually filed under Functions (or Number & Quantity) on the enhanced ACT, not Algebra. Defensible as 'exponential expressions in context', but a reviewer could move it.

AM22A-06.stem_issue: Tagged 'quadratic' but the t^2 terms cancel and the equation is linear (100t = 130); the item is easier than its tag and does not test quadratics. Also 'thrown from the ground' is idealised (h0 = 0) - fine.

bounds.bound: The thrown ball moves much faster than the dropped ball throughout, so it covers more than half the 130 ft gap: meeting height > 65

estimation_bound.estimate: Gap closes at 100 ft/s -> t = 1.3 s; dropped ball falls 16*1.3^2 ~ 16*1.7 ~ 27 -> ~103

neighbouring_setup.what: Forgets to square t: 130 - 16*1.3 = 109.2. 65.0 is the naive midpoint (equal speeds)
neighbouring_setup.bound_kills: 109.2 not killed without work; 65.0 killed by the faster-ball bound

AM22A-06.free_elimination: Relative-motion insight (gravity cancels, gap closes at 100 ft/s) makes the item one line; this is the intended algebraic cancellation, not a flaw, but it means the item is easier than a genuine quadratic.
AM22A-06.duplicate_note: Classic 'thrown up / dropped down, where do they meet' physics template.
